newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Red Cross finds refugees in bad state in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross finds refugees in bad state in Zaire.

text.p: Thousands of refugees from conflict in eastern Zaire have trekked 200 km (120 miles) to the west and suffer from diarrhoea, malaria and malnutrition, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said on Tuesday.

An ICRC delegate came across 8,000 to 10,000 of the refugees near the Zairean town of Shabunda and found they were Rwandans and Burundians from refugee camps near the town of Uvira on the shores of Lake Tanganyika, a Red Cross statement said.

A separate mission by the medical charity Medecins sans Frontieres, after a flight over eastern Zaire on Tuesday, estimated that at least 50,000 people were along the road which runs northwest towards the city of Kisangani.
The ICRC said: "Most of the refugees were in very bad condition, suffering from diarrhoea, malaria and malnutrition.
"There are indications that large groups of women, children and elderly people are in the surrounding forest regions under very difficult living conditions."

The report was the most detailed yet on the state of Rwandan refugees who wandered deep into Zaire after fighting broke out around the camps in October between the Zairean army and Zairean rebels of Rwandan Tutsi origin.

More than 600,000 of the Rwandan refugees have gone home to Rwanda but others, including some of the Hutu militants who killed up to one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda in 1994, have disappeared into the Zairean countryside.
Some of them do not want to go home for fear of prosecution or revenge attacks by relatives of the people they killed.

The ICRC pulled out of the eastern town of Kindu and the northeastern city of Kisangani last week for security reasons. The ICRC delegate flew to Shabunda on Sunday from the south Zairean mining city of Lubumbashi.

"At this stage the ICRC will concentrate its efforts on ensuring the survival of the refugees it has located. Emergency food, in the form of protein biscuits, and medical supplies, will be flown in as from today," the statement said.

"The ICRC does not want its activities to favour the establishment of new camps and is discussing with the authorities and the UNHCR (United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees) the future of these populations," it added.
Nicholas Louis, a Medecins sans Frontieres officer in Kisangani, said he flew 30 km (20 miles) beyond Walikale town on Tuesday on a trip to assess the number of people in need.

"We reckoned about 50,000 people between Lubutu and the furthest point we went. What we noticed is that there are very very children among them...Some people are lying by the roadside but not a huge number," he told Reuters by phone.
"You can't see anything off the road. It's the thickest forest I have ever seen so we can't say anything about people who might have gone into the forest," he added.
Louis said the local people seemed to have abandoned the villages along the road and refugees had moved in, sometimes in concentrations of more than one thousand.

The ICRC statement did not say who held the town of Shabunda but the rebels, known as the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, have not named the town in the list of the towns they say they have captured.
The rebels have captured a strong of towns extending 500 km (300 miles) close to Zaire's eastern border, from Mambasa in the north to the mining centre of Kamituga in the south.
